column4: Section's “وأما السائل” protects the one who comes to ask; 80:8 itself stages the visitor “من جاءك يسعى.” Its neighbors 80:9–10 complete the scene: he fears God, while the Prophet is distracted from him.

This neighbor to 80:8 identifies the visitor as one who “يخشى,” completing the portrait of the person who comes seeking. That detail makes the rebuke in 80:10 especially pointed beside the section's protection of the asker.

The section commands that the asker not be rebuked (“فلا تنهر”). 80:10 itself reproaches the Prophet for turning away from the visitor; neighboring 80:8–9 show that he came striving and fearing God, completing the contrast with the commanded welcome.

The section's root note says “سأل” covers asking to know as well as asking to receive. Here people ask the Prophet about Dhul-Qarnayn, and he is to answer by reciting a remembrance of him (“سأتلوا عليكم منه ذكرا”), joining the questioner with the narrator.

The section's verb “تَنْهَرْ” means to rebuke. In 17:23 children are told not to rebuke their parents (“ولا تنهرهما”) and instead to speak nobly; this supplies a concrete boundary for the same harsh verbal act.

The section leaves “السائل” open to a person asking for material help. 51:19 names “السائل والمحروم” among those with a due share in the believers' wealth, showing why a petitioner at the door is owed consideration.

The section's material reading of “السائل” is made concrete by 70:24: believers keep a known share in their wealth. Its neighbor 70:25 identifies the recipients as the petitioner and deprived person, completing the connection.

This ayah names “السائل” and the deprived person as recipients of a known share in wealth; its neighbor 70:24 establishes that share. It directly supports the section's reading of the asker as someone seeking material help.

The section says “سأل” can mean asking for something or asking about it. The question “ماذا ينفقون” is answered with whom to support, including orphans and the poor; this joins the questioner's voice to material care.

The section explicitly treats the question about orphans as a second kind of inquiry. Here “يسألونك عن اليتامى” receives an answer that reforming their affairs is best, showing a questioner met with guidance rather than rebuke.

The section includes someone who comes to ask about God among the meanings of “السائل.” Here worshippers ask the Prophet about God, and the reply says “فإني قريب” and promises response to the caller; the question is met with nearness.
The section's “سائل” can be one who asks for something. After Moses' long supplication, God answers “قد أوتيت سؤلك يا موسى”; this is a direct instance of a request received and granted.

The section allows “السائل” to be a learner asking a question. 16:43 directs those who do not know to ask people of remembrance (“فاسألوا أهل الذكر”), giving that sense of the protected questioner a concrete place in seeking knowledge.

Like 16:43, this ayah tells those who do not know to ask people of remembrance (“فاسألوا أهل الذكر”). It directly supports the section's learner who comes with a question, rather than a material petition.

The section's ban on rebuking a petitioner concerns the words used around need. 2:263 says a kind word and pardon are better than charity followed by injury (“قول معروف ومغفرة خير”); it makes gentle speech part of giving itself.

The section commands speech about the Lord's gift and protects the person who asks from rebuke. 2:264 warns that charity is voided by reminders and injury (“بالمن والأذى”), marking the boundary between grateful telling and speech that wounds a recipient.

When someone must turn away from people seeking the Lord's mercy, 17:28 still commands “فقل لهم قولا ميسورا”—a gentle, accessible word. This gives the section's asker a specific model of response when the request cannot be granted.
The section's “السائل” can be someone asking for material help. 2:177 names “السائلين” among those to whom the righteous give wealth, putting care for the asker into the same account of goodness.

The section lets “السائل” mean a needy person who asks at the door. 2:273 describes poor people who “لا يسألون الناس إلحافا” despite their need; it adds the less visible petitioner who does not press people for help.

The section gives Joseph's words as an example of attributing kindness to God: “وقد أحسن بي” when God brought him out of prison. His reunion account names the good he received, illustrating what it means to tell of a Lord's favor.
The section quotes God's command to Jesus to remember His favor on him and his mother (“اذكر نعمتي عليك وعلى والدتك”). It is a direct parallel to publicly acknowledging a received divine blessing.

The section calls this the same reminder given to believers. 3:103 says “واذكروا نعمت الله عليكم” and recalls that God joined their hearts after enmity; recounting the favor includes naming its change in their relationship.

The section presents Moses turning a received blessing into speech: “رب بما أنعمت علي” precedes his pledge not to aid wrongdoers. The ayah shows a blessing being acknowledged aloud and shaping what the speaker will do.

The section contrasts naming the Lord as giver with the claim “هذا لي” in 41:50. When Solomon receives the throne, he says “هذا من فضل ربي”; the explicit attribution makes this a positive counterpart to claiming a favor as one's own.

The section commands the Prophet to tell of “نعمة ربك.” 16:53 says that whatever favor people have is from God (“وما بكم من نعمة فمن الله”), giving the attribution that the command asks the speaker to preserve.

The section calls this a crooked account of favor: after relief, the speaker says “هذا لي,” claiming the gift as his own. It reverses the command to name it as “نعمة ربك” and shows what grateful telling corrects.

The section's root note connects “نعمة” with blessing, and 102:8 says people will be questioned about “النعيم.” This places telling of favor beside accountability for what was received, a boundary to the section's command.

The section notes that the root of “بنعمة” also yields “نعم,” an affirmative answer. In 7:44 the people of the Fire answer “نعم” when asked whether they found God's promise true, giving that response word its explicit Quranic scene.
The section's lexical note links “نعمة” with the response “نعم.” In 37:18 “نعم” answers whether resurrection will occur, making the yes-sayer a distinct voice in a scene of questioning.

The section commands the Prophet to tell of the Lord's favor. 2:40 commands Israel to remember “نعمتي التي أنعمت عليكم”; the repeated call makes recollection of received favor a public act of speech and memory.
Like 2:40, this ayah commands Israel to remember the favor bestowed on them (“اذكروا نعمتي”). Its repetition reinforces the section's movement from receiving favor to naming it.
This renewed address to Israel again says “اذكروا نعمتي التي أنعمت عليكم.” It is another direct command to recall a divine favor, the act that the section's “فحدث” turns into telling.

The section's command to tell the Lord's favor meets a direct call to remember “نعمة الله عليكم.” Here the reminder is paired with what God revealed of scripture and wisdom, specifying what the community is to keep in its account.

This ayah commands believers to remember “نعمت الله عليكم” together with their covenant. It is another explicit communal recollection of God's favor, matching the section's move from private gift to voiced recognition.
Believers are told to remember God's favor when a people meant to reach out against them and God restrained their hands. This gives the section's command a concrete account of protection to tell.

Moses tells his people to remember God's favor when He saved them from Pharaoh's people. Like the section's sequence of shelter, guidance, and provision, this is a narrated deliverance offered as a divine favor.

The address “اذكروا نعمة الله عليكم” recalls the day the enemy forces came and God sent wind and unseen forces. This is a concrete communal story of protection that gives content to speaking of the Lord's favor.
The section commands telling of the Lord's favor; 35:3 tells people to remember God's favor and asks who else provides from heaven and earth. The ayah joins naming the blessing with naming its giver.

The section contrasts proper telling of the Lord's favor with a false claim of ownership. 16:83 says people recognize God's favor and then deny it (“يعرفون نعمت الله ثم ينكرونها”), a direct reversal of voicing it.

The section presents three blessings in sequence before commanding their telling. 14:34 says God's favors cannot be enumerated (“لا تحصوها”); it widens that short sequence into an uncountable abundance to acknowledge.
Like 14:34, this ayah says God's favors cannot be counted (“لا تحصوها”). It gives the section's command to tell of favor an open-ended subject rather than a closed list.
The section connects blessing with a voiced response; 16:114 commands people to eat from God's provision and “اشكروا نعمت الله.” It makes gratitude the fitting answer to a received favor.

After the answer to Moses' request in 20:36, God says “ولقد مننا عليك مرة أخرى” and begins recalling an earlier favor. This neighbor completes the section's connection between a granted request and an account of prior blessing.

The section notes that asking can be mutual (“تساءلوا”). 37:27 says the guilty turn to one another, asking and blaming each other; this is a contrary use of mutual questioning, unlike a petitioner who should not be rebuked.

The section's dictionary note says people may ask one another. 52:25 shows the people of Paradise turning to each other to ask, making mutual conversation a peaceful scene rather than the need or rebuke of 93:10.
The section notes the reciprocal form of asking (“تساءلوا”). 78:1 uses it of people asking one another about the great news, showing the questioner's voice can circulate among a group.

The section says telling is a form of Quranic address and quotes “وهل أتاك حديث موسى.” The ayah opens Moses' story by asking the Prophet whether its account has reached him, making narrated report itself a mode of address.

The section includes the learner who asks within “السائل.” Here people ask the Prophet about the new moons and receive an answer about time-markers for people and pilgrimage, a specific example of a question being answered.

This question to the Prophet concerns fighting in the sacred month; the answer distinguishes its gravity from other wrongs. It shows the section's “sā'il” as an inquirer who receives an explanation, not merely a person asking for goods.

People ask about intoxicants and gambling, and the reply weighs their sin against their benefit (“إثمهما أكبر من نفعهما”). This is a particular knowledge-seeker's question within the section's broad sense of “السائل.”
The question “ماذا أحل لهم” asks the Prophet what is lawful, and he answers with good things and trained hunting animals. It gives a concrete case of the learner's question being answered.
People ask the Prophet about the Hour, but he answers that its knowledge rests with his Lord. This shows a questioner met with an answer that sets a boundary on what can be told.

The question “يسألونك عن الأنفال” asks about the division of spoils, and the answer calls for God-consciousness and reconciliation. This combines a request about material goods with an answer that redirects the question toward conduct.

The questioners ask whether the warning is true, and the Prophet is told to answer “إي وربي إنه لحق.” This joins the section's inquirer with an affirmative spoken reply, though the ayah uses “إي” rather than the source's lexical “نعم.”

People ask about the spirit; the answer says it is from the Lord's command and that human knowledge is limited. This is a specific question answered with a boundary, like 7:187's question about the Hour.
People ask the Prophet about the mountains, and the answer describes them being scattered away. It is another concrete instance of the questioner's voice receiving an answer in the Quran.

People ask about the Hour, and the answer says its knowledge is with God and that it may be near. The question receives both a limit and a warning, specifying the section's question-and-answer relation.
The question “متى مرساها” asks when the Hour will arrive; the answer says its timing belongs to the Lord and the Prophet is only a warner. It gives another specific boundary in response to an asker.
This uses the same address as 20:9, “هل أتاك حديث موسى,” which the section cites as an example of Quranic telling. Its repetition shows that the story of Moses is introduced through direct address.
The verse opens Abraham's encounter with the honored guests using “هل أتاك حديث ضيف إبراهيم.” This repeats the Quranic address-form of “حديث” that the section connects with narration.
The question “هل أتاك حديث الجنود” introduces the armies' story. It repeats the section's Quranic address-form in which a “حديث” is brought to the listener.
The verse asks “هل أتاك حديث الغاشية,” introducing the account of the Overwhelming Event. It is another direct instance of the “حديث” address-form named in the section.

The section defines “حديث” as speech from which one thing follows another. 12:6 promises Joseph the interpretation of “الأحاديث”; the plural ties the root to accounts and unfolding meanings, though here it concerns dreams.
Joseph is promised “تأويل الأحاديث” in this account of his life. The root's sense of unfolding report or interpretation meets the section's account of speech that brings one thing after another.
Joseph asks God to teach him the interpretation of “الأحاديث” after the story's events have unfolded. This links the root's narrative sense to a speaker making sense of what has happened.

The section notes the dictionary description of a person whose speech is good (“حسن الحديث”). 41:33 praises the one whose speech is best, calling to God and acting righteously; it gives a concrete Quranic counterpart for speech valued by its content.

The section says the root in “خير” can name asking which of two things is better. After the Israelites ask for other food, 2:61 asks whether they would exchange what is better for what is lower (“أتستبدلون الذي هو أدنى بالذي هو خير”), making that evaluative choice explicit.

The section's dictionary note connects “خير” with seeking the better of two things. 28:68 uses the related choice form “يختار” and “الخيرة,” while saying creation and choice belong to God; it makes choice the boundary of human asking.

The section's “السائل” can be someone requesting something; 70:1 describes a “سأل سائل” asking for a punishment to befall. This is a stark reversal of the vulnerable petitioner seeking help, showing that the same asking word can carry a hostile demand.

The section says not to rebuke the asker, and the surrounding surah 93:9 also protects the orphan. 107:2 describes the one who repulses an orphan (“يدع اليتيم”), the opposite treatment of a vulnerable person and a sharp boundary for the section's commands.

Where the section forbids harshness toward the asker and its surah context protects the orphan, 107:3 condemns failing to urge the feeding of the poor (“ولا يحض على طعام المسكين”). It supplies the material neglect that accompanies the opposite posture.
